text: High blood pressure is called the silent killer. Most people who have it feel completely fine. So how can something you can't feel damage your heart, your brain, and your kidneys? Stay with me, because the answer is surprising.
First, what counts as high? For adults, blood pressure of one thirty over eighty or higher is high blood pressure, also called hypertension. Remember, either number can be too high.

Why does it happen? In most adults, there is no single cause. It builds up over years, with age, family history, too much salt, extra weight, not moving enough, alcohol, and smoking. This is called primary hypertension. Sometimes another problem, like kidney disease, causes it. That's secondary hypertension.

Now let's zoom inside an artery. Every heartbeat pushes blood against the wall. When the pressure is always high, the wall is under constant strain. Over time, it gets stiff and thick, and the inside gets narrower. Tiny tears make it easier for plaque to build up.

Now look at the heart. Pushing against high pressure every beat is hard work. So the left ventricle muscle grows thicker, just like a muscle at the gym. But a heart wall that's too thick gets stiff, and over time, the heart can fail.
So, why the silent killer? Because all of this damage happens quietly. Most people have no symptoms at all, for years. The only way to know is to measure your blood pressure.
Left untreated, high blood pressure raises the risk of a heart attack, a stroke in the brain, heart failure, and kidney damage. It can even harm the tiny blood vessels in the eyes.

Very high readings, above one eighty over one twenty, are an emergency warning sign. If there are symptoms like chest pain, a severe headache, confusion, or trouble seeing, call your local emergency number right away.

The good news? It can be controlled. Eat less salt, and more fruits and vegetables. Move for at least one hundred and fifty minutes a week. Keep a healthy weight, limit alcohol, and don't smoke. And when needed, doctors add medicines that relax the vessels or remove extra fluid.

So remember three things. One thirty over eighty or higher is high. It's silent, so check it. And it can be controlled. Now that you know how high pressure strains the heart, watch the next video, to see what happens when the heart starts to fail.
